claim: NFPA 72 requires an average Speech Transmission Index of at least 0.50 per Acoustically Distinguishable Space, with at least 90% of measurement locations at or above 0.45, for emergency communication systems.
source_title: NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code (2022 edition), Chapter 24 — Emergency Communications Systems
source_citation: NFPA 72 (2022 ed.), Chapter 24 and Annex D, National Fire Protection Association, Quincy, MA
page_or_section: Chapter 24 with intelligibility guidance in Annex D
supporting_excerpt: Intelligibility acceptance criterion widely paraphrased across the industry as average STI >= 0.50 per ADS with at least 90% of measurement points >= 0.45; equivalent CIS ~0.70.
airport_or_entity: US-wide code applicability including MWAA jurisdictions
caveat: NFPA 72 is a paywalled consensus standard; the specific numerical threshold is widely paraphrased in industry literature. Verify against the operator's licensed copy before board-facing use.

claim: IEC 60268-16 Annex G identifies STI 0.50 as an appropriate target for voice-address (VA) systems.
source_title: IEC 60268-16 — Sound System Equipment, Part 16: Objective Rating of Speech Intelligibility by Speech Transmission Index
source_citation: IEC 60268-16, Annex G, International Electrotechnical Commission, Geneva
supporting_excerpt: Codes and application standards typically recommend a minimum STI of 0.45 or 0.50; IEC 60268-16 Annex G suggests STI 0.50 as an appropriate target value for VA systems.
caveat: Paywalled IEC standard; the STI 0.50 target for VA is confirmed in multiple secondary technical sources but should be verified against a licensed copy for design-manual language.

claim: ACRP Research Report 175 recommends a Speech Transmission Index target of 0.50 for airport terminal public address, with an acceptable range of 0.46 to 0.53.
source_title: ACRP Research Report 175: Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems
supporting_excerpt: STI range 0.46 to 0.53 is acceptable for voice address, with a target of 0.50.
denominator: per listener position in airport terminal PA zones
caveat: The full ACRP 175 PDF failed to render for direct extraction; the STI target and range are confirmed in multiple secondary technical summaries. Design-manual language should cite the ACRP publication directly.

claim: ACRP Report 175 recommends maintaining SNR of at least 10 dB(A) with a minimum STI of 0.45 for public address broadcasts in pier-style airport departure lounges.
source_title: Exploring Factors Influencing Speech Intelligibility in Airport Terminal Pier-Style Departure Lounges
supporting_excerpt: For pier-style departure lounges, ACRP 175 recommends maintaining an SNR of 10 dB(A) and a minimum STI of 0.45 for public address broadcasts to ensure announcements are clearly audible to passengers.
denominator: announcement level minus ambient LAeq at listener position
caveat: Peer-reviewed paper citing ACRP 175; verify the exact wording in ACRP 175 for design-manual reference.

claim: Basic acoustic ceiling tile installation for commercial construction costs $5 to $15 per square foot, with premium acoustical systems reaching $17 to $22 per square foot.
source_title: Acoustical Ceiling Cost Per Square Foot: Price Guide 2026
supporting_excerpt: Basic tiles with standard grid often cost $3 to $6 per sq ft installed, while premium acoustical options with advanced moisture resistance and better NRC values can reach $7 to $12 per sq ft; premium installations $17-$22 per sq ft.
denominator: per square foot of ceiling area
caveat: Commercial secondary source (contractor pricing guide), not airport-specific bid data. Airport airside conditions typically add cost premiums due to badging, escort, and after-hours work.

claim: Retrofit acoustic panel treatment for commercial spaces typically costs $18 to $45 per square foot installed.
source_title: Acoustic Retrofit vs. New Construction: Cost & Time Guide
supporting_excerpt: Retrofit acoustic panel treatment for commercial spaces typically ranges from $18-$45 per square foot installed, depending on product specification, coverage density, and project complexity, which is notably higher than new drop ceiling installation but faster to implement.
denominator: per square foot of treated area
caveat: Commercial secondary source. Retrofit-in-operating-airport premiums (night work, escort) not captured; treat as a floor, not a ceiling.

claim: London City Airport's silent terminal policy, implemented August 2016, removed flight and gate announcements from the terminal PA except for emergencies and made all flight information available via screens, mobile, and social channels.
source_title: Silent Airport Policy — London City Airport
supporting_excerpt: London City Airport implemented a 'silent terminal' policy, which means only essential announcements are delivered via the public-address system. In the case of emergency, announcements are made.
caveat: Operator statement of policy, not a measured intelligibility or missed-boarding result. Passenger satisfaction claims cited by operator lack published methodology.

claim: Helsinki Airport has operated a 'silent airport' policy since 2015 in which no flight or passenger announcements are made in the terminal except at the departure gate and in emergencies.
source_title: Silent airport announcement policy — Helsinki Airport (via Aviation24 and Finavia)
supporting_excerpt: Helsinki Airport has been a silent airport since 2015. This means no flight or passenger announcements will be made in the terminal. However, at the departure gate and when there is an emergency, announcements are still broadcast.
caveat: Operator narrative via trade press. No published intelligibility measurement or missed-boarding data located.

claim: Schiphol Airport describes itself as a 'silent airport' with virtually no announcements, with information shown exclusively on FIDS and the app; 2025 passenger satisfaction reached 3.84/5, the highest score in ten years excluding the COVID period.
source_title: Schiphol in 2025: quieter aircraft, more satisfied travellers and solid financial results
supporting_excerpt: The 2025 passenger satisfaction score reached its highest level in ten years (excluding the COVID period), with passengers giving an average rating of 3.84 on a scale of 5.
caveat: Operator-published composite score; does not isolate the announcement-reduction contribution from other satisfaction drivers. Not a direct intelligibility or channel-redundancy measurement.

claim: Concourse E at Washington Dulles (IAD) is approximately 435,000 square feet with 14 gates, initial phase scheduled to open in 2026.
source_title: Concourse E — Dulles Next
supporting_excerpt: The concourse is roughly 435,000 square feet with 14 gates.
caveat: Operator project page; scope may be updated as construction proceeds.

claim: The Dulles Concourse E project has been publicly cited at costs ranging from approximately $500 million to approximately $900 million across reporting dates and phasing.
source_title: Dulles Airport Is Getting A Brand New Concourse (DCist)
supporting_excerpt: Reported project costs vary across sources and dates: ~$500M to ~$900M for the first phase.
denominator: Concourse E first phase total project cost
caveat: Range reflects reporting date and phasing differences rather than a single audited figure. Board-adopted budget amendments would be the authoritative source.

claim: MWAA, USDOT, and United Airlines announced on July 29, 2026 a decade-long transformation of IAD of $20 billion or more, including concourse modernization and expansion, accelerated AeroTrain expansion, upgraded baggage handling, expanded CBP facilities, and preservation of the Saarinen main terminal.
source_title: Inside the $20B+ Plan to Remake Washington Dulles International Airport
supporting_excerpt: July 29, 2026 announcement of a decade-long $20B+ transformation of IAD, with elements as summarized.
caveat: Treat July 29, 2026 announcement paraphrases as provisional until underlying Board action, program budget amendment, and airline-consent documents are located.

claim: MWAA's projected cost per enplanement rises to $20.71 by 2030 (pre-July-2026 program announcement), per the airport context packet's summary of MWAA 2025 disclosures.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — Quiet-by-Design Standards for MWAA Terminals
supporting_excerpt: MWAA's 2025 Official Statement projected cost per enplanement rising to $20.71 by 2030 before the July 29, 2026 announcement of a $20B+ Dulles program.
caveat: Context packet paraphrases the 2025 Official Statement; the primary MWAA disclosure should be cited in a board packet.

claim: MWAA plans approximately $5.5 billion of new debt across 2025 to 2028, with adjusted debt per O&D enplanement projected to peak near $400 in 2028.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — Quiet-by-Design Standards for MWAA Terminals
supporting_excerpt: MWAA plans approximately $5.5 billion of new debt between 2025 and 2028. Adjusted debt per origin-and-destination enplanement is projected to peak near $400 in 2028.
units: USD millions and USD per O&D enplanement
denominator: MWAA airport system revenue-bond debt stack
caveat: Context packet paraphrase used to inform the debt-service factor in Exhibit E6; primary MWAA disclosure should be cited in a board packet.

claim: IAD carried approximately 29.01 million passengers in 2025, up 6.4% year-over-year, including 10.53 million international passengers.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — Quiet-by-Design Standards for MWAA Terminals
supporting_excerpt: IAD: 29.01 million passengers, up 6.4% year-over-year; 10.53 million international passengers, roughly 36%+ international share.
caveat: Context packet consolidating MWAA public traffic disclosures.

claim: DCA carried approximately 24.89 million passengers in 2025, down 5.4% year-over-year, with MWAA attributing the decline to the January 29, 2025 midair collision aftermath, softening government-related travel, and a 43-day federal shutdown.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — Quiet-by-Design Standards for MWAA Terminals
supporting_excerpt: DCA: 24.89 million passengers, down 5.4% year-over-year. MWAA attributed the decline to the aftermath of the January 29, 2025 midair collision, softening government-related travel demand, and the 43-day federal shutdown.
caveat: Context packet consolidating MWAA public traffic disclosures.

claim: Airline passenger no-show rates industry-wide fall in the 5% to 18% range, with a 2019 study reporting a 14.4% average and an August peak of 18.3%.
source_title: Flight No-Show: What It Means & What to Do
supporting_excerpt: The accepted range for no-shows is between 5 and 15%, though a 2019 study showed that on average, 14.4% of passengers don't show up for their flight. In August, the no-show rate peaked at 18.3%.
caveat: Industry no-show rate conflates true no-shows (never arrived at the airport) with missed-at-gate. Do not use this range as the operational-downside control number for a reduced-PA regime.

claim: A new 15-year MWAA Airline Use and Lease Agreement took effect January 1, 2025, replacing the prior agreement, and carried at execution an approximately $9 billion capital construction program split roughly $6.99B at IAD and $2.39B at DCA.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — Quiet-by-Design Standards for MWAA Terminals
supporting_excerpt: A new 15-year Airline Use and Lease Agreement took effect January 1, 2025, replacing the prior agreement. At execution the agreement carried an approximately $9 billion capital construction program: approximately $6.99 billion at IAD and approximately $2.39 billion at DCA.
caveat: Any MWAA standard that materially affects airline gate systems, tenant paging rights, or airline-controlled hold-room audio engages majority-in-interest and consultation provisions of the use agreement.

claim: MWAA maintains a seven-volume 2020 Design Manual, described as a mandatory guide with the force of law on the airport property, updated annually, with airport-specific supporting volumes for IAD and DCA and Specifications edited from MASTERSPEC for MWAA use.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — Quiet-by-Design Standards for MWAA Terminals
supporting_excerpt: MWAA maintains a seven-volume 2020 Design Manual, plus Specifications and Estimating and Scheduling Standards, issued by the MWAA Office of Engineering. The Design Manual is described by MWAA as a mandatory guide with the force of law on the airport property, updated annually.
page_or_section: Section 7 (MWAA Design Manual and standards apparatus)
caveat: The context packet does not verify whether the current Design Manual already contains binding acoustic, PA-zoning, STI, or LAeq requirements. Absence of a public quiet-by-design standard is the operative fact for this run.

claim: ANSI/ASA S12.60 stipulates background noise levels not exceeding 35 dBA (approximately NC 27) in core learning spaces, a benchmark useful only as a design reference for MWAA sensory-quiet zones.
source_title: ANSI/ASA S12.60 Part 1 — American National Standard Acoustical Performance Criteria, Design Requirements, and Guidelines for Schools
source_citation: ANSI/ASA S12.60 Part 1, Acoustical Society of America, current edition
page_or_section: Section on core learning space background sound level
supporting_excerpt: Background noise limits for classrooms not exceeding 35 dBA (about NC 27) in core learning areas.
airport_or_entity: US-wide standard, applied here only as a benchmark for MWAA-defined sensory-quiet zones
caveat: ANSI standard is paywalled; the 35 dBA / NC 27 figure is widely cited in secondary sources. Do NOT interpret this as an ambient target for main terminal areas — it is only a reference benchmark for defining low-stimulation zones within MWAA.
